text: At Lomekwi in Kenya, early humans chipped stones into tools about 3.3 million years ago, the oldest stone tools known.
At Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, early humans had fires that left burned bone and plant ash about 1 million years ago.
At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, early humans cooked fish from a lake about 780,000 years ago.
src: Zohar and colleagues, 2022, Nature Ecology & Evolution

text: At Kalambo Falls in Zambia, early humans cut notches to join two logs into a structure at least 476,000 years ago.
At Schöningen in Germany, hunters made long wooden spears and used them on horses at least 200,000 years ago.
At Katanda in Congo, people carved barbed bone points, likely for catching big catfish, about 90,000 years ago.
In Africa, lice that live only in clothes split from head lice at least 83,000 and maybe 170,000 years ago, a clue people wore clothes.
src: Toups and colleagues, 2011, Molecular Biology and Evolution

text: At Madjedbebe in northern Australia, people were living about 65,000 years ago, after crossing open sea to get there.
At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people strung tiny shells with holes in them as beads about 75,000 years ago.
At Leang Karampuang cave in Sulawesi, Indonesia, people painted a wild pig and three human-like figures at least 51,200 years ago.
On Muna Island in Indonesia, someone blew paint around a hand on a cave wall at least 67,800 years ago, the oldest known cave art.
At Hohle Fels Cave in Germany, people played flutes made of vulture bone and mammoth ivory at least 35,000 years ago.
At Abri du Maras in France, Neanderthals twisted plant fibres into a three-ply cord more than 40,000 years ago.
At Campitello in Italy, early humans used birch-bark tar as glue on stone tools about 200,000 years ago.
src: Mazza and colleagues, 2006, Journal of Archaeological Science

text: At Diepkloof Rock Shelter in South Africa, people carved patterns on ostrich eggshell water flasks about 60,000 years ago.
At Xianrendong Cave in China, people who hunted and gathered made clay pots about 20,000 years ago, the oldest known pottery.
At Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, hunter-gatherers baked flat bread from wild grains about 14,400 years ago, before farming began.
At Oberkassel in Germany, a sick puppy was cared for and buried with two people about 14,200 years ago, among the oldest known dogs.
src: Janssens and colleagues, 2018, Journal of Archaeological Science

text: At Shillourokambos on Cyprus, a cat was buried beside a person about 9,500 years ago, a sign cats and people were close.
In the Zagros Mountains of Iran, people began herding and taming wild goats about 10,000 years ago.
In the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East, people began planting wild wheat and barley about 11,500 years ago.
In the Yangtze River valley of China, people were growing rice by about 8,000 years ago, slowly turning it into a crop.
In the Balsas River valley of Mexico, people were grinding and growing maize about 8,700 years ago.
At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, people carved and raised huge T-shaped stone pillars between about 11,600 and 10,200 years ago.
src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Göbekli Tepe

text: At Çatalhöyük in Turkey, about 9,000 years ago, people lived in packed mud-brick houses with no streets and climbed in through the roof.
src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Neolithic Site of Çatalhöyük

text: At Jiahu in China, traces of silk were found in tombs about 8,500 years old, the oldest known signs of silk.
In Poland, farmers used clay pots full of little holes as strainers to make cheese more than 7,000 years ago.
At Belovode in Serbia, people heated green rocks in fire to get copper metal about 7,000 years ago, the oldest known smelting.
src: Radivojević and colleagues, 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science

text: At Varna in Bulgaria, people were buried with gold jewelry about 6,500 years ago, the oldest big hoard of worked gold.
In the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, a wooden wheel with its axle survived in the mud for about 5,200 years, among the oldest wheels found.
src: City Museum of Ljubljana (MGML), The Wheel - 5,200 Years

text: In the Somerset Levels of England, people built the Sweet Track, a plank walkway over a swamp, in 3807 or 3806 BC.
src: English Heritage, Prehistoric travel and networks

text: From the grasslands by Russia's Volga and Don rivers, the horses we ride today spread across Asia and Europe about 4,000 years ago.
In Mesopotamia, now Iraq, people began writing by drawing pictures and numbers on clay tablets about 5,300 years ago.
src: Spar, 2004, The Origins of Writing, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

text: At Wadi el-Hol in Egypt, workers carved some of the oldest known alphabet letters on rock about 3,900 years ago.
src: Darnell and colleagues, 2005, Annual of the American Schools of Oriental Research

text: In the Middle East and southeast Europe, iron began to replace bronze for tools and weapons about 3,200 years ago.
src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, What is the Iron Age?

text: In Lydia, now western Turkey, people made the first coins from electrum, a mix of gold and silver, more than 2,600 years ago.
src: British Museum, A History of the World in 100 Objects (BBC)

text: At Fangmatan in China, a scrap of hemp paper with a map drawn on it was found in a tomb about 2,150 years old.
src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Today in History: April 28

text: In China, a Buddhist scroll called the Diamond Sutra was printed in 868 CE, the oldest dated printed book.
On Wrangel Island in the Arctic, the last woolly mammoths lived on until about 4,000 years ago.
Across the world, giant ice sheets were at their biggest between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago, in the last Ice Age.
At Provadia-Solnitsata in Bulgaria, people boiled salty spring water in clay pots to make salt, from about 7,600 to 6,400 years ago.
In Mesopotamia, now Iraq, craftspeople first made glass by melting sand with soda and lime about 4,000 years ago.
src: Corning Museum of Glass, Origins of Glassmaking

text: At Denisova Cave in Siberia, people sewed with tiny bone needles that had eyes for thread about 40,000 years ago.
In Chauvet Cave in France, people drew lions, horses and rhinos on the walls between about 37,000 and 34,000 years ago.
